Last time we met a pressure that does not need heat: the electron degeneracy
pressure that stops a brown dwarf from collapsing before it can ignite. This
time we take it seriously, because it is what holds up a **white dwarf**, the
object most stars leave behind when they die. Degeneracy pressure behaves
unlike any pressure we have met so far. It does not care about temperature, so
a white dwarf can cool forever without shrinking. **The more massive a white
dwarf is, the smaller it is.** And because nothing can move faster than light,
there is a **largest mass** that degeneracy pressure can ever hold up. That
limit, the Chandrasekhar mass, is the first step on the road from stars to
black holes.

## How to read this lecture

**The main reading for this lecture is Kutner, Chapter 10, Section 10.4**,
which is in the Canvas Files under *Reading Material*, both as a PDF and as an
accessible Word document. These notes do three jobs: they say where a white
dwarf comes from, they draw out two consequences that Kutner's section contains
but does not dwell on — that heavier white dwarfs are smaller, and that above
the Chandrasekhar mass nothing we have met so far can stop a collapse — and
they give you exercises on all of it.

### The readings

| Kutner section | read it for |
|:---|:---|
| §10.4.1 Electron degeneracy | where degeneracy pressure comes from, and why it depends on density but not on temperature |
| §10.4.2 Properties of white dwarfs | how dense white dwarfs are, the mass–radius relation, and why they take so long to cool |
| §10.4.3 Relativistic effects | why there is a maximum mass, the Chandrasekhar limit |
| §10.1.1 and §10.3 *(optional)* | how a star like the Sun gets from the main sequence to a white dwarf: the red giant stage and the planetary nebula |

You can skip §10.1.2 and §10.2.

Two things to know while you read. **Kutner writes $h/2\pi$ throughout**, and
so does your constants sheet; it is the same constant physicists often write
as $\hbar$. And **Kutner's mass–radius relation, his equation 10.14, gets the
way a white dwarf's size depends on its mass right, but the number it gives is
far too small.** Use it for how the radius *scales*, not for the radius itself.
There is more on this below, in [The heavier, the smaller](#sec-heavier).

## Where a white dwarf comes from

A star spends most of its life on the main sequence, fusing hydrogen into
helium in its core. When the hydrogen in the core runs out, the core contracts
and heats up, and the star's outer layers swell until it becomes a **red
giant**. In a star like the Sun the core eventually gets hot enough to fuse
helium into carbon and oxygen, and when that fuel runs out too, the core
contracts once more. **It never gets hot enough for the next stage of fusion.**

Meanwhile the swollen outer layers are only loosely held by gravity, and the
star drives them off. The expanding shell of gas is lit up by the hot core it
leaves behind, and we see it as a **planetary nebula** — a name left over from
how these clouds looked in small telescopes, with nothing to do with planets.
What is left in the middle is the bare core: carbon and oxygen, typically a
little over half the mass of the Sun, about as big as the Earth, very hot, and with no fusion
going on inside it. **That is a white dwarf.**

Kutner puts the dividing line at about $5\,M_\odot$.
More recent measurements, which match white dwarfs in star clusters to the
stars they came from, trace white dwarfs back to stars born with as much as
$7.5\,M_\odot$ [@cummings2018], and the usual round number today is about
$8\,M_\odot$. Lecture 11's initial mass function says that covers all but
about six stars in every thousand.

Nothing is left to heat the core, and nothing is left to make new heat. So
what stops it from contracting forever? Gas pressure cannot: the thermal
pressure of a gas is $P = nkT$, and a star that is not making energy is losing
it, so $T$ can only fall. The answer is a pressure that does not depend on
temperature at all.

## A pressure that ignores temperature

Kutner §10.4.1 builds degeneracy pressure from two pieces of quantum mechanics.
The **exclusion principle** says that no two electrons can be in the same
state, so in a dense gas most of the electrons are forced into states of high
momentum, far above what their temperature alone would give them. The
**uncertainty principle** says the same thing another way: squeeze the
electrons close together, and the spread in their momenta has to grow. Fast
electrons push hard on whatever they hit, and that push is **degeneracy
pressure**.

Two features of Kutner's result, his equation 10.11, carry this whole lecture.

- **It depends on density and not on temperature.** Squeeze the gas and the
  pressure rises; cool it and nothing happens. That is the opposite of a gas
  in an ordinary star.
- **It rises steeply with density**, as

  $$
  P_{\mathrm{deg}} \propto \rho^{5/3} .
  $$ {#eq-pdeg}

  This holds as long as the electrons move slowly compared with light. Kutner
  §10.4.3 shows what changes when they do not.

::: {.callout-tip .resolution collapse="true" title="Think about what happens to a white dwarf's size as it cools"}
Nothing happens to it. A white dwarf is held up by degeneracy pressure, which
does not depend on temperature, so as it radiates away its heat and cools, its
size stays the same. It fades and reddens at a fixed radius. Compare a normal
star, which is held up by thermal pressure: if it could not replace the energy
it radiates, it would have to contract.
:::

::: {.content-visible when-format="html"}

### Exercises {#sec-exercises-pressure}

1. Sirius B, the white dwarf companion of the brightest star in the sky, has a
   mass of $1.018\,M_\odot$ and a radius of $0.008098\,R_\odot$
   [@bond2017eri]. What is its average density? What mass of it would fill a
   teaspoon, about $5\ \mathrm{cm^3}$?

   ::: {.callout-note .help-solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
   The average density is the mass divided by the volume of a sphere,
   $\rho = M / \tfrac43 \pi R^3$. Convert the mass and radius to grams and
   centimeters first, arranging each fraction so that the solar unit cancels:

   $$
   \begin{aligned}
   M &= 1.018\,M_\odot
        \times \frac{1.9891 \times 10^{33}\ \mathrm{g}}{1\,M_\odot} \\[0.8em]
     &= 2.025 \times 10^{33}\ \mathrm{g} , \\[0.8em]
   R &= 0.008098\,R_\odot
        \times \frac{6.9598 \times 10^{10}\ \mathrm{cm}}{1\,R_\odot} \\[0.8em]
     &= 5.636 \times 10^{8}\ \mathrm{cm} .
   \end{aligned}
   $$

   Now substitute, with the units attached and no arithmetic yet:

   $$
   \rho = \frac{2.025 \times 10^{33}\ \mathrm{g}}
               {\tfrac43 \pi \left(5.636 \times 10^{8}\ \mathrm{cm}\right)^{3}} .
   $$

   The units are $\mathrm{g} / \mathrm{cm^3}$. *Do the units make sense?* A
   density is a mass per volume, so yes. Now the numbers: the volume is
   $7.499 \times 10^{26}\ \mathrm{cm^3}$, so

   $$
   \rho = 2.7 \times 10^{6}\ \mathrm{g\,cm^{-3}} .
   $$

   A teaspoon holds

   $$
   \begin{aligned}
   5\ \mathrm{cm^3} \times 2.7 \times 10^{6}\ \mathrm{g\,cm^{-3}}
     &= 1.35 \times 10^{7}\ \mathrm{g} \\[0.8em]
     &= 1.35 \times 10^{7}\ \mathrm{g}
        \times \frac{1\ \mathrm{t}}{10^{6}\ \mathrm{g}} \\[0.8em]
     &= 13.5\ \mathrm{t} ,
   \end{aligned}
   $$

   where t is a metric ton. A teaspoon of Sirius B weighs about as much as
   two elephants. Its radius, $5{,}600\ \mathrm{km}$, is a little smaller than
   the Earth's.
   :::

2. Kutner estimates the momentum of an electron in a degenerate gas as
   $p \approx (h/2\pi)\, n_e^{1/3}$, where $n_e$ is the number of electrons
   per cubic centimeter. The electrons are moving at close to the speed of
   light once $p$ reaches about $m_e c$.

   a. At what electron density does that happen?
   b. What mass density is that, for carbon or oxygen, which have one electron
      for every two nucleons? Use $\rho = 2 m_p n_e$.
   c. How does it compare with the average density of Sirius B, from
      exercise 1?

   ::: {.callout-tip .help-hint collapse="true" title="Hint, and the answer"}
   Set $(h/2\pi)\, n_e^{1/3} = m_e c$ and solve for $n_e$ by cubing both sides.
   The answers are $n_e = 1.7 \times 10^{31}\ \mathrm{cm^{-3}}$ and
   $\rho = 5.8 \times 10^{7}\ \mathrm{g\,cm^{-3}}$, about 20 times Sirius B's
   average density. Sirius B's center is several times denser than its
   average, so its electrons are well on the way to moving at the speed of
   light — which will matter in [Why there is a largest mass](#sec-chandrasekhar).
   :::

3. The Sun's core is at about $1.5 \times 10^{7}\ \mathrm{K}$ and a white
   dwarf's interior at about $10^{7}\ \mathrm{K}$, much the same. Why, then, is
   the Sun's core held up by thermal pressure and a white dwarf by degeneracy
   pressure?

:::

## The heavier, the smaller {#sec-heavier}

Pile more mass onto an ordinary star and it gets bigger. Pile more mass onto a
white dwarf and it gets **smaller**. The reason is that degeneracy pressure can
only answer extra weight by being squeezed to a higher density.

A star in balance needs enough pressure at its center to hold up the weight of
everything above it. For a star of mass $M$ and radius $R$, the pressure it
needs goes as $G M^2 / R^4$, and its density goes as $M / R^3$. Set the pressure
from @eq-pdeg equal to the pressure needed, and the radius and mass have to be
related by

$$
R \propto M^{-1/3} .
$$ {#eq-mr}

That is the content of Kutner's equation 10.14, with the constants stripped
away. With slow electrons, doubling a white dwarf's mass shrinks it by a factor of
$2^{1/3} = 1.26$, to about four fifths of its size.

```{python}
#| label: fig-mass-radius
#| fig-cap: "The radius of a white dwarf against its mass. The dashed orange line is @eq-mr, the relation for electrons moving slowly compared with light. The solid blue line includes the effect of the electrons approaching the speed of light, using the approximation of @nauenberg1972; it falls to zero radius at the Chandrasekhar mass. The dots are three nearby white dwarfs whose masses are measured from their orbits in binary systems and whose radii are measured from their light [@bond2017eri]. The dotted gray line along the bottom is Kutner's equation 10.14 taken literally. All curves are for a white dwarf of carbon and oxygen."
#| fig-alt: "A line chart of white dwarf radius in kilometers, from 0 to 16,000, against mass in solar masses, from 0.2 to 1.6. A dashed orange curve falls slowly from about 15,000 kilometers at 0.2 solar masses to about 7,800 at 1.45. A solid blue curve starts on top of the dashed one at low mass, bends below it above about half a solar mass, and falls steeply to zero radius at 1.45 solar masses, where a vertical gray line is labeled Chandrasekhar mass. A horizontal dotted line at about 6,400 kilometers is labeled Earth's radius. Three black dots lie close to the blue curve: 40 Eri B at 0.57 solar masses and about 9,100 kilometers, Procyon B at 0.59 and about 8,600, and Sirius B at 1.02 and about 5,600. A dotted gray line labeled Kutner equation 10.14 runs along the bottom of the chart, at a few hundred kilometers."
#| fig-height: 4.0

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.2, 4.0))

R_SUN_KM = 6.9598e5          # his constants sheet, in km
R_EARTH_KM = 6378.17
MU_E = 2.0                   # carbon and oxygen: two nucleons per electron
M_CH = 5.816 / MU_E**2       # Nauenberg (1972), in solar masses


def r_nauenberg(m):
    """Zero-temperature white dwarf radius in km, Nauenberg (1972)."""
    x = m / M_CH
    return 0.0225 / MU_E * x**(-1/3) * np.sqrt(1 - x**(4/3)) * R_SUN_KM


def r_slow(m):
    """The same, with the electrons treated as slow: R proportional to M^(-1/3)."""
    return 0.0225 / MU_E * (m / M_CH)**(-1/3) * R_SUN_KM


# Kutner's equation 10.14 (with the corrected 4 pi^2), his constants sheet
h, m_e, m_p, G = 6.6262e-27, 9.1096e-28, 1.6726e-24, 6.6732e-8
M_SUN = 1.9891e33
K_1014 = 2 * h**2 / (4 * np.pi**2 * m_e) * (0.5 / (4 * m_p))**(5/3) / G


def r_kutner(m):
    return K_1014 / (m * M_SUN)**(1/3) / 1e5


m = np.linspace(0.2, M_CH, 600)
ax.plot(m, r_slow(m), color=ORANGE, ls="--", zorder=3,
        label=r"electrons slow, $R \propto M^{-1/3}$")
ax.plot(m, r_nauenberg(m), color=BLUE, zorder=4,
        label="electrons approaching light speed")
ax.plot(m, r_kutner(m), color=MUTED, ls=":", zorder=3)
ax.annotate("Kutner eq. 10.14", (0.95, r_kutner(0.95)),
            textcoords="offset points", xytext=(0, 5),
            fontsize=9.5, color=MUTED)

ax.axhline(R_EARTH_KM, color=MUTED, ls=":", lw=1.2, zorder=2)
ax.annotate("Earth's radius", (0.21, R_EARTH_KM), textcoords="offset points",
            xytext=(0, 4), fontsize=9.5, color=MUTED)

ax.axvline(M_CH, color=AXIS, lw=1.2, zorder=2)
ax.annotate("Chandrasekhar\nmass", (M_CH, 10800), textcoords="offset points",
            xytext=(-6, 0), ha="right", fontsize=9.5, color=INK2)

# Bond, Bergeron & Bedard (2017), Table 1: mass (Msun), radius (Rsun)
stars = {"40 Eri B": (0.573, 0.01308), "Procyon B": (0.592, 0.01232),
         "Sirius B": (1.018, 0.008098)}
offsets = {"40 Eri B": (-8, 6), "Procyon B": (8, -12), "Sirius B": (8, 4)}
for name, (mass, rad) in stars.items():
    ax.plot(mass, rad * R_SUN_KM, "o", color=INK, markersize=6, zorder=5)
    ax.annotate(name, (mass, rad * R_SUN_KM), textcoords="offset points",
                xytext=offsets[name], ha="right" if offsets[name][0] < 0 else "left",
                fontsize=9.5, color=INK, zorder=5)

ax.set_xlim(0.2, 1.6)
ax.set_ylim(0, 16000)
ax.set_xlabel(r"mass ($M_\odot$)")
ax.set_ylabel("radius (km)")
ax.legend(loc="upper center", fontsize=9.5)
plt.show()
```

@fig-mass-radius shows the relation, and three real white dwarfs that follow
it. At low mass the two curves agree. At higher mass they part, because the
electrons in a heavy white dwarf are squeezed so hard that they approach the
speed of light, and then the white dwarf shrinks faster still. That is the
subject of the next section.

::: {.callout-warning .textbook-watch title="Textbook watch (Kutner): equation 10.14 gives the right scaling and the wrong size"}
Put $1\,M_\odot$ into Kutner's equation 10.14 and it gives a radius of about
$400\ \mathrm{km}$ — some fifteen to twenty times smaller than the Earth-sized
white dwarf of his own Example 10.2, a page earlier. The
scaling, $R \propto M^{-1/3}$, is right. The number is not, and the reason is an
approximation Kutner makes on the way: he sets the pressure from the **average**
density of the star. The center of a white dwarf is about six times denser
than its average, and because the pressure goes as $\rho^{5/3}$, the center can
push about twenty times harder than the average density suggests. **So use
equation 10.14 for how the radius changes with mass, and take the radius
itself from a measured white dwarf**, like the ones in @fig-mass-radius.

**An early version of the course constants sheet has a typo in this relation**:
it prints $h^2/4\pi m_e$ where $h^2/4\pi^2 m_e$ belongs, which makes the radius
it gives larger by a factor of $\pi$. If your copy has $4\pi$ there, correct it.
:::

::: {.content-visible when-format="html"}

### Exercises {#sec-exercises-heavier}

1. Use @eq-mr to predict how the radius of Sirius B ($1.018\,M_\odot$) should
   compare with that of 40 Eri B ($0.573\,M_\odot$). The measured radii are
   $0.008098\,R_\odot$ and $0.01308\,R_\odot$. Is Sirius B smaller than the
   prediction or larger? Using @fig-mass-radius, explain why.

   ::: {.callout-tip .help-hint collapse="true" title="Hint, and the answer"}
   Take the ratio of the two versions of @eq-mr, so the unknown constant
   cancels. The prediction is $R_{\mathrm{Sirius\,B}} / R_{\mathrm{40\,Eri\,B}}
   = (1.018/0.573)^{-1/3} = 0.83$; the measured ratio is $0.62$. Sirius B is
   smaller than @eq-mr predicts, because at its mass the electrons are already
   moving fast enough for relativity to matter, and the solid curve in
   @fig-mass-radius has bent below the dashed one.
   :::

2. According to @eq-mr, by what factor would a white dwarf's mass have to grow
   for its radius to halve? A typical white dwarf has $0.6\,M_\odot$. What
   mass does @eq-mr say it would need to reach half its radius, and what is
   wrong with that answer?

   ::: {.callout-note .help-answer collapse="true" title="Answer"}
   Eight times: $R \propto M^{-1/3}$, so halving $R$ takes $2^3 = 8$ times the
   mass, which would be $4.8\,M_\odot$ — far above the Chandrasekhar mass,
   where no white dwarf can exist. @eq-mr assumes the electrons stay slow, and
   in a heavy white dwarf they do not. In @fig-mass-radius the real curve
   reaches half the radius of a $0.6\,M_\odot$ white dwarf at only about
   $1.15\,M_\odot$.
   :::

3. A white dwarf and a main-sequence star each gain a little mass. Which of
   them gets bigger, and which gets smaller? Explain the difference in terms
   of what kind of pressure holds each one up.

:::

## Why there is a largest mass {#sec-chandrasekhar}

As a white dwarf gets heavier and smaller, its electrons are squeezed closer
together and pushed to higher momenta, until they are moving at close to the
speed of light. Then something changes. An electron's momentum can keep
growing, but its speed cannot pass $c$, so it cannot hit the walls of its
container any more often. The pressure still rises with density, but more
slowly: Kutner §10.4.3 shows that it goes as

$$
P_{\mathrm{deg}} \propto \rho^{4/3}
$$ {#eq-pdeg-rel}

instead of $\rho^{5/3}$.

That small change in the exponent has a large consequence. With the pressure
of @eq-pdeg-rel, **the radius drops out of the balance altogether**, which
Kutner shows on the way to his equation 10.17. There is only one mass at which
the balance can hold. A white dwarf lighter than that can find a radius where
its pressure holds it up. A white dwarf heavier than that cannot: squeezing it
smaller raises the pressure it has, but it raises the pressure it needs by just
as much, so it never catches up. **Gravity wins, and the star collapses.**

That mass is the **Chandrasekhar mass**,

$$
M_{\mathrm{Ch}} \approx 1.4\,M_\odot .
$$ {#eq-mch}

The exact number depends on details of the calculation — Kutner quotes
$1.44\,M_\odot$, and the simplest careful calculation gives $1.46\,M_\odot$ —
so the round number astronomers use is $1.4\,M_\odot$. It depends on what the white dwarf is made of, through
the number of nucleons per electron: the value here is for helium, carbon and
oxygen, which all have two.

Subrahmanyan Chandrasekhar found the limit in 1930, at the age of 19, working
out the calculation on the ship taking him from India to graduate school in
England [@chandrasekhar1931]. It is the solid curve of @fig-mass-radius
reaching zero radius: no white dwarf is found above it, and none can exist.

### What happens above the limit

Kutner defers this to his next chapter, and so will we, but the outline is
worth having now, because it is where this course has been heading. The core of
a very massive star is built up, fusion stage by fusion stage, until it is
iron, and once an iron core grows past the Chandrasekhar mass, electron
degeneracy pressure cannot hold it. It collapses in about a second. What
catches it, if anything does, is a new pressure: **neutron degeneracy
pressure**, the same physics with neutrons in place of electrons, and the
result is a **neutron star**. Neutron stars have a maximum mass too. **Above
that there is no pressure we know of that can stop the collapse, and the
result is a black hole.** Those are the next two lectures.

::: {.content-visible when-format="html"}

### Exercises {#sec-exercises-chandrasekhar}

1. A white dwarf of $1.4\,M_\odot$, just under the limit, has a radius of about
   $1{,}800\ \mathrm{km}$. What is its Schwarzschild radius, and how many times
   larger than that is the white dwarf?

   ::: {.callout-note .help-answer collapse="true" title="Answer"}
   $r_S = 4.1\ \mathrm{km}$, so the white dwarf is about 430 times larger than
   its own Schwarzschild radius. Even at the Chandrasekhar mass a white dwarf
   is nowhere near being a black hole: when it collapses, it has a long way to
   fall.
   :::

2. Kutner's equation 10.17 shows that the Chandrasekhar mass goes as
   $(Z/A)^2$, the square of the number of electrons per nucleon. For carbon
   and oxygen $Z/A = 1/2$, which gives $1.44\,M_\odot$. What is the
   Chandrasekhar mass for a core of iron-56, which has 26 protons and 30
   neutrons?

   ::: {.callout-note .help-answer collapse="true" title="Answer"}
   About $1.24\,M_\odot$. Iron has fewer electrons per nucleon than carbon, so
   there are fewer electrons to share the load, and the limit is lower.
   :::

3. Explain, without equations, why the fact that electrons cannot travel
   faster than light leads to a maximum mass for a white dwarf.

:::

## Summary

| idea | result | why it matters |
|:---|:---|:---|
| Where white dwarfs come from | the bare core of a star born with less than about $8\,M_\odot$ | nearly every star ends this way |
| Degeneracy pressure | $P_{\mathrm{deg}} \propto \rho^{5/3}$, independent of temperature | a white dwarf holds its size while it cools forever |
| Mass and radius | $R \propto M^{-1/3}$ | heavier white dwarfs are smaller |
| The Chandrasekhar mass | $M_{\mathrm{Ch}} \approx 1.4\,M_\odot$ | when the electrons approach $c$, $P_{\mathrm{deg}} \propto \rho^{4/3}$, and above this mass no radius can hold the star up |

Every star in this course so far has been a contest between gravity and a
pressure, and in every case the pressure could win by the star changing its
size. The Chandrasekhar mass is the first case where it cannot. Next time we
follow the stars that are too massive to end as white dwarfs, to the collapse
of their cores and the supernovae that follow.
